title: Attention
theme: What do I notice, and what do I merely assume?
move: Use a staff-approved short local route. Record ten observations, three inferences and one uncertainty. Read legend, scale and orientation at three agreed stops. Practise posture, spacing, footwork and a verbal stop cue with a coach. Use solo movement before any paired task. Complete the two coached strength sessions within fieldcraft; record an appropriate variation, feedback and recovery.
think: Plato, Apology: selected passages on examination and responsibility; Laozi, Tao Te Ching: Chapters 1, 2 and 11. Compare what argument reveals with what naming may conceal.
make: Investigations 1 and 2: How does a representation shape a journey? What can we infer without reaching a summit? Scale, ratios and uncertainty. Extend to alternative route geometries and an uncertainty range. Similar triangles; tan(theta) = height difference / horizontal baseline. Derive and critique the construction.
give: Agree a learner council with responsibility for discussion norms, fair duties and an approved project choice.
evidence: A 400–600-word opening argument, two annotated passages and a tutorial revision.
prompt: What do I notice, and what do I merely assume? Write an initial answer, the strongest objection and a revised claim. Use a named passage or observed evidence; distinguish what you know from what you assume.

title: Discipline
theme: When does restraint make us stronger?
move: At a reserved serviced campsite, practise shelter setup, layout, dry storage and shared chores. The lead teaches the site’s actual food and wildlife procedures. Use staff-approved cooking equipment only. On suitable mats, use coach-chosen low-resistance balance tasks; no throws or submissions. Partners continuously agree the level of contact. Complete the two coached strength sessions within fieldcraft; record an appropriate variation, feedback and recovery.
think: Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics II.1–6; Confucius, Analects 2.4, 4.17, 12.1 and 15.24. Read Dhammapada II, verses 21–32 as a short third perspective on attention and conduct.
make: Investigations 3 and 4: How could the sky help us find direction? What does a changed glacier outline establish? Angles, rotation and proportional time; the idealised relation between celestial-pole altitude and observer latitude. Distance / elapsed time; scale correction and an uncertainty range. Advanced work compares more dates or competing rate models.
give: Make a fictional resource budget and explain one opportunity cost.
evidence: An Essay 1 draft connecting a precise textual claim with one observed practice; distinguish habit from conformity.
prompt: When does restraint make us stronger? Write an initial answer, the strongest objection and a revised claim. Use a named passage or observed evidence; distinguish what you know from what you assume.

title: Evidence
move: Choose an approved route with simple observation stops. Measure sections against the printed map; explain why pace, grade and weather change a time estimate. Watch a short technical demonstration and distinguish what was seen from what was inferred. Practise the selected correction slowly. Complete the two coached strength sessions within fieldcraft; record an appropriate variation, feedback and recovery.
think: Wang Yangming’s knowledge/action exchange recorded by Xu Ai, paired with Hume, Enquiry IV on experience and inference. Preserve their different questions and historical settings.
make: Investigations 5 and 6: How can we explain Medicine Lake? Which model explains the cooling curve? Change in storage = total inflow minus total outflow over an interval. Track volume and time units; identify unknown terms. Rates, graphs and an exponential-cooling extension using supplied logarithm tables; discuss conduction, convection and evaporation.
give: Give a peer one precise criticism that improves an experiment.
evidence: Essay 1 revised to 1,200–1,500 words or equivalent; answer a counterexample in tutorial.
prompt: What would change my mind? Write an initial answer, the strongest objection and a revised claim. Use a named passage or observed evidence; distinguish what you know from what you assume.

title: Freedom
move: Pairs explain the next short section while the guide retains control. Rotate leader, navigator, companion-check and recorder roles. Keep the party together. Rehearse assertive verbal boundaries, stepping away and seeking help through non-contact scenarios. No simulated ambush or coercive role-play. Complete the two coached strength sessions within fieldcraft; record an appropriate variation, feedback and recovery.
think: Mill, On Liberty II; Wollstonecraft, Vindication II. Examine the institutions and educational opportunities needed for meaningful independence.
make: Investigations 7 and 8: What does Miette’s mineral list actually tell us? What would count as evidence after fire? Mass concentration, amount of substance, ionic charge and units. Identify measurement-date and completeness limitations. Sampling bias, proportions, variability and confounding. Compare results under two sample-selection rules.
give: Test a capstone claim; record a learner-council decision about a shared non-financial resource.
evidence: A 600–800-word Essay 2 proposal, an opposing argument represented fairly and a learner-council decision record.
prompt: What makes disagreement productive? Write an initial answer, the strongest objection and a revised claim. Use a named passage or observed evidence; distinguish what you know from what you assume.

title: Responsibility
theme: What do I owe to a place and to other people?
move: Repeat the readiness gate. Set up in a reserved serviced site; assign fair chores, verify communications and practise the agreed regroup location. Design a short safe sequence from previously approved movements, then have the coach review it before practice. Complete the two coached strength sessions within fieldcraft; record an appropriate variation, feedback and recovery.
think: Selected passages from Ostrom, Governing the Commons, Chapter 3, alongside Tagore, Gitanjali 35–36 and local published mapping history. Test an institutional rule against a concrete shared-resource problem.
make: Investigations 9 and 10: What does gaining height cost in a model? How could a useful explanation fail? Delta E = mgh; power = energy / time; opportunity cost and sensitivity to assumptions. Choose geometry, rates, concentration or uncertainty analysis appropriate to the question. Explain the model’s domain.
give: Test the artifact with a consenting peer or confirmed host and record a revision.
evidence: Essay 2 draft; a proposed rule with monitoring, revision and a fair account of who bears its costs.
prompt: What do I owe to a place and to other people? Write an initial answer, the strongest objection and a revised claim. Use a named passage or observed evidence; distinguish what you know from what you assume.

title: Contribution
theme: What can I now explain, do and give?
move: Revisit a comparable accessible route or indoor map problem. Compare preparation and decisions with Week 1. Explain the difference between better judgment and simply better conditions. Practise the final sequence at an agreed pace. Show the solo or adapted equivalent. Include a stop and restart decision. Complete the two coached strength sessions within fieldcraft; record an appropriate variation, feedback and recovery.
think: Douglass, Narrative VI–VII; Epictetus, Enchiridion 1, 5 and 30. Ask what requires personal practice and what requires changing institutions.
make: Investigations 11 and 12: What can we now investigate with intellectual honesty? Can your explanation survive a serious question? Select and defend a suitable model. Advanced work may compare models or test robustness; a new equation is not required. Check units, model assumptions, uncertainty and logical inference. Explain one thing the evidence cannot establish.
give: Present the artifact and explain your individual contribution at the Jasper Commons Hearing.
evidence: Essay 2 revised to 1,200–1,500 words or equivalent; individual defence and a justified continuation plan.
prompt: What can I now explain, do and give? Write an initial answer, the strongest objection and a revised claim. Use a named passage or observed evidence; distinguish what you know from what you assume.
